claims.text: Intrinsic randomness in the bcc high-entropy alloy creates local lattice distortions.
The local lattice distortions maintain a uniformly high density of states at the Fermi level.
The alloy supports isotropic, weak-coupling s-wave superconductivity.
Electron-phonon coupling is responsible for pairing in this alloy.
The disorder-generated electronic environment enables superconductivity despite substantial chemical disorder.
The starting material is a homogeneous, randomly distributed, single-phase bcc alloy similar to (TaNb)0.67(HfZrTi)0.33.
Mild annealing can reduce local chemical disorder and lattice distortion without causing phase separation.
High-configurational-entropy lattice distortions produce multifractal electronic states.
Random atomic arrangements produce spatial variations in bond lengths and bond angles.
These bond-scale variations preserve electronic coherence rather than suppressing it.
The relevant Ta-Nb-Hf-Zr-Ti high-entropy alloy can show a sharp zero-resistance transition near 7.7 K.
The relevant alloy can show a strong diamagnetic response beginning near 7.6 K, consistent with bulk superconductivity.
The superconducting state is robust against moderate magnetic-field perturbations.
Applied magnetic field lowers the superconducting transition temperature.
Reducing local disorder by heat treatment will lower Tc or increase magnetic-field sensitivity.
Configurational entropy is associated with pressure robustness of superconductivity in high-entropy systems.
The proposed mechanism applies only while the material remains single-phase bcc and lacks major segregation.
Loss of the multifractal electronic states upon disorder suppression defines a limit of the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis attributes favorable Tc and superconducting robustness to disorder and predicts that reducing disorder will degrade them, whereas PMC9329343 reports comparable disorder at two compositions and explicitly excludes a disorder-driven explanation for the observed Tc variations.
